opus-5.5.text:
Math is a really natural fit for that kind of structure, because that's how mathematicians actually work. When you attack a hard problem, you don't write one long, linear chain of reasoning from start to finish. You break it apart. You say, "If I can prove this lemma, and this other estimate holds, then the main theorem follows." Each piece can be worked on somewhat independently, and then you stitch them together.

Sub-agents let an AI system mirror that. Instead of one model trying to hold an entire proof in a single context window, which gets very long and fragile, you have an orchestrator that decomposes the problem into sub-goals and hands them off. One agent might search the literature or the library for relevant results, another might try to formalize a lemma, another might hunt for a counterexample to check whether a conjecture is even true. They can run in parallel, and the failures are local. If one branch gets stuck, you haven't lost the whole attempt.

What makes this especially powerful in math, compared with other domains, is verification. If you're working in a formal language like Lean, every sub-agent's output can be checked by the proof assistant. You don't have to trust that the piece is correct. That turns the coordination problem into something much more tractable. In software or in open-ended research, when you combine work from many agents, errors compound and it's hard to know which part went wrong. In formal math, the checker tells you exactly which step fails, so you can send that piece back for another try.

So for me it's a scaling story along a different axis. People have scaled pre-training and then test-time compute in a single stream of thought. Sub-agents let you scale breadth: more exploration, more parallel attempts, more specialization, all anchored by a verifier that keeps the whole system honest. I think that's how you get from solving competition problems, which fit in a few pages, to real research mathematics, where a proof might have dozens of interlocking lemmas and take a human months or years.

There are still open questions. The hard part is the decomposition itself, choosing which lemmas are the right ones to aim for, and that's where a lot of mathematical taste lives. But that's exactly what makes it exciting to work on.

r001.rationale: The response describes decomposing proofs into sub-goals and delegating work, but does not identify a process segment as experience from which an AI system can learn.

r002.rationale: It mentions specialized sub-agent tasks and parallel exploration, but does not propose expanding sub-agents’ tool-use choices to scale learning from mathematical problem-solving experience.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it is that mathematics itself is already organized like a team of specialists, and sub-agents let us mirror that structure.

When a human mathematician attacks a hard problem, they're not doing one monolithic thing. They're exploring several candidate approaches, checking lemmas, searching the literature, running small computations, trying to find counterexamples, and then stepping back to decide which thread is actually promising. Those are different cognitive modes, and in a research group they're often done by different people. If you ask a single model to hold all of that in one context window, it tends to blur the modes together. It starts believing its own partial proofs, or it commits too early to one path because it can't afford to explore five at once.

Sub-agents break that bottleneck in a few concrete ways.

First, parallelism. Hard math problems have a huge branching factor at the level of strategy. Do you attack this combinatorially, probabilistically, algebraically? With sub-agents you can send independent explorers down each branch simultaneously and only pay attention to the ones that come back with something. That's much closer to how progress actually happens than a single linear chain of thought.

Second, separation of generation and verification. One of the biggest failure modes of models in math is that the same reasoning process that produced an argument is also judging it, so errors are correlated. If you have a dedicated verifier agent, ideally one that is adversarial, whose entire job is to find the gap, you decorrelate those errors. And when you can hand a proof to a formal system like Lean, the verifier isn't even a model anymore; it's a compiler. That's where I think the structure becomes really powerful, because now the orchestrator can treat "did this check" as ground truth and iterate.

Third, context hygiene. Mathematical arguments are long and fragile. If a model has spent eighty thousand tokens on a dead end, that history pollutes everything that follows. A sub-agent lets you encapsulate that: the explorer comes back with a two-paragraph summary, "this approach fails because of this obstruction," and the orchestrator keeps a clean, high-level view. You get the lesson without the debris.

And fourth, which is maybe the deepest reason, it's the only architecture I can see that scales with compute in a sensible way. If you want to throw a thousand times more compute at a problem, you can't just make a chain of thought a thousand times longer; the model loses the thread. But you can run a thousand explorers, a hierarchy of orchestrators, and verifiers at every level. The structure gives you a place to put the compute. That's essentially what the mathematical community does over decades, just slowed down by publication cycles. We're trying to compress that into hours.

I'd also be honest about what's hard. The orchestrator has to be genuinely good at taste, at knowing which partial result is worth pursuing, and that's still the scarce ingredient. Communication between agents is lossy. And on truly open problems, decomposition itself is the hard part; nobody hands you the subgoals. But I'd rather build on a structure that reflects how mathematics is actually done than on one that asks a single model to be the entire research community at once.

r001.rationale: The response describes exploration, verification, and lessons from failed approaches, but does not identify these as experience from which an AI system learns.

r002.rationale: It discusses parallel approaches and tools such as computation, literature search, and Lean, but does not propose that broadening sub-agents’ tool-use choices scales learning from problem-solving experience.

astra-6.text:
I think math has a natural structure for dividing up work. When you’re trying to prove something, you might explore a few approaches, test examples, look for counterexamples, or isolate a lemma. Sub-agents could pursue those directions in parallel, so you’re not committing all your computation to one line of reasoning too early.

But the important part is how those efforts come back together. Ten agents repeating the same mistake aren’t much better than one. You want useful diversity, clear subproblems, and a way to check whether each result actually supports the larger proof. Formal verification can help with that when the problem is expressed formally.

So the promise is that you can spend additional computation on exploration and checking, with a coordinating agent assembling the pieces. The challenge is making that coordination productive enough that adding agents leads to better mathematics.

sol-6.1.text:
I think math has a natural structure for this: you have a big problem, but making progress often means breaking it into smaller claims, trying different approaches, and checking whether each step actually works. Sub-agents give you a way to explore those directions in parallel. One agent might look for a useful lemma, another might try to construct a counterexample, and another might check the proof for gaps.

The interesting part is that those roles can complement each other. If everyone follows the same approach, you don’t necessarily gain much. But if agents pursue genuinely different ideas and communicate the useful pieces, you can cover more of the search space.

Of course, you still need a way to verify the results and bring them together. Ten plausible arguments don’t make a correct proof. So I see the promise as combining parallel exploration with rigorous checking, while keeping the coordination cost low enough that adding agents actually helps.
